appraisal_events.evidence: ma mère aurait bien voulu que je m'en tinsse à celle de Galland... du sentiment qu'étant une femme, d'une part elle manquait, croyait-elle, de la compétence littéraire qu'il fallait... ma mère ne pouvait douter de la condamnation que ma grand'mère eût prononcée contre le livre de Mardrus.
appraisal_events.explanation: The mother is shown doubting her own literary authority as a woman and continually deferring to what she imagines her deceased mother would have judged, subordinating her taste to the grandmother's remembered, unquestionable standard; the free-indirect 'croyait-elle' keeps this a reported self-doubt rather than a flat narrator verdict.

appraisal_events.evidence: il écrivait un vrai nektar, avec un k, ce qui lui permettait de ricaner au nom de Lamartine.
appraisal_events.explanation: Bloch's Hellenizing spelling affectation, undertaken as a self-important 'devoir religieux' of literary talent, is presented with clear narratorial irony that makes his pretension look absurd.

status_effects.explanation: Her self-doubt about her own literary competence and her deference to her dead mother's remembered opinion weaken her standing as an independent judge of the narrator's reading.

The grandmother's remembered taste and judgments (fidelity to 'Carlovingiens', objection to distorted names) are treated as the enduring, unquestioned standard the mother measures herself against, posthumously reinforcing her authority.
His pedantic Hellenized orthography is mocked as pretentious affectation, undercutting his intellectual credibility within the passage.

ambiguities: The mother's self-assessment of lacking literary competence is marked by 'croyait-elle' (free indirect style), so it is her own internalized belief rather than a clear-cut narrator endorsement; this affects how strongly E1 should be read as diminishment versus neutral reporting of her perspective.
